title: Nice, not needed
hook: Stoics prefer health and wealth but don't stake their happiness on them

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four virtues, wisdom, courage, justice and self-control. Your line was one excellence, four sides.

Two days ago the Stoics said health and money aren't truly good. Easy to say from a marble bench. So does a Stoic shrug at a broken leg? Turn down a raise? Live on cold water and gravel? No. The reason is a careful piece of sorting: the difference between something you'd like and something you need. A warm coat on a cold day. A good night's sleep. A full fridge. Nice. Very nice. The Stoic word for them is adiaphora.
screen: `SO A STOIC SHRUGS AT A BROKEN LEG?` → `NO.` → `ADIAPHORA.`

segments.voice: Adiaphora is Greek for indifferents, things that don't make a difference. Not to your comfort; there they make a big difference. They make no difference to whether you're a good person. Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself: all indifferent in that one sense. But the Stoics sorted the indifferents. Some are preferred: health over sickness, enough money over poverty, friends over loneliness. It's natural and sensible to pick those, and a Stoic will. Others are dispreferred, and it's sensible to avoid them. Zeno explained the word preferred with a picture from a royal court, which Cicero passes on. At court, the ministers and nobles are promoted, placed near the throne. But none of them is the king. Health and money are like that: high in rank, never the ruler. Only character sits on the throne. Seneca was a very rich man, and in his essay On the Happy Life he answers critics who threw that at him. Roughly: the wise person may own wealth, but wealth must not own him. Epictetus gives the gentlest picture of all, in his Handbook: behave in life as at a banquet. When a dish comes around to you, reach out and take a polite share. If it passes you by, don't grab at it. If it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch across the table. Enjoy what's in front of you. Just don't stake your happiness on the next plate.
screen: `ADIAPHORA — INDIFFERENTS.` · `PREFERRED, AND DISPREFERRED.` · `NEAR THE THRONE, NEVER THE KING.` · `TAKE A SHARE AT THE BANQUET.` · then, large: `NICE, NOT NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Choose one comfort that's with you right now, the chair under you, a warm drink, the quiet in the room, and enjoy it fully for a few breaths. Then gently imagine it gone: the chair harder, the drink cold, the room loud; you'd still be you. Come back to the comfort, and hold it a little more lightly.
Adiaphora. Greek for indifferents: things like health and wealth that are worth preferring but don't make you good or bad. Today's word.
Your line: take a polite share. Near the throne, never the king. See you tomorrow.
